newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: No trade sanction but NZ-U.S. drugs row rumbles on.
newsitem.headline: No trade sanction but NZ-U.S. drugs row rumbles on.

text.p: U.S. drug companies this week failed to have New Zealand put on an exporters "priority watch list" for its pharmaceutical subsidy policies but are likely to keep up the pressure, an industry lobby group said on Friday.

"The issues are still there. I'm sure the American companies will continue to place pressure at a senior trade level," said Kim Miles, chief executive of the Researched Medicines Industry (RMI), which includes many U.S. firms among its members.
"I imagine come the end of the year or early next year, there will be consideration given to whether or not they make an updated submission," he told Reuters.
But the agency at the centre of the row, New Zealand's pharmaceutical management agent Pharmac, said it was pleased Washington had seen though the drugmakers' "sabre-rattling".
"It is good to see that fairness has been the winner in what really is an industry having a tantrum because it cannot get its own way," Pharmac general manager David Moore told Reuters.
Pharmac decides which medicines receive government funds allocated to the New Zealand public health system.

Big U.S. research-based drugmakers had asked the U.S. Trade Representative to impose the watch list sanction on New Zealand, arguing that Pharmac's policies denied them access to the New Zealand market.
The RMI considered the firms had a valid case.
"Companies face delays in being able to get access into the New Zealand market because of some of the ways Pharmac operates," Miles told Reuters earlier this week.
U.S. drugmakers claim Pharmac will not subsidise a new medicine unless it is offered at a lower price than currently available competing medicines in the same therapeutic class.
"This is tosh and we told the U.S. government so. We sent a full response to the U.S. Trade Representative to counter allegations which we believe were made by the RMI," Moore said.
"Pharmac will subsidise drugs if they offer an advantage to New Zealand patients and doctors. This may be a new use, better side-effects profile, or a lower price."
Had the priority watch sanction been imposed, both Pharmac and the RMI agree it could have resulted in retaliation against New Zealand exporters to the United States.

"If New Zealand was trying to get more favourable entry for something into the States, undoubtedly this question would sit on the table and would be discussed before anything we wanted was considered," Miles said.
Moore said some of Pharmac's policies were "leading edge" and that he suspected the drug companies were afraid of a domino effect occurring internationally.
British Columbia in Canada had already adopted some of the same techniques for managing pharmaceuticals, and Pharmac expected other countries to look at the New Zealand system.
The New Zealand pharmaceutical market is currently worth about NZ$729 million (US$502.8 million), of which the U.S. market share is around NZ$211 million, or 29 percent.
